A cheap vegan high-protein meal plan: what it costs

Vegan eating is often called expensive. For protein it is not, at moderate targets: dried lentils and beans are among the cheapest protein sources in any shop. What limits a vegan plan is not price but room, because the cheap protein arrives with a lot of carbohydrate. A solver shows both.

Open the free cheapest meal plan optimizer and pick "Vegan" under eating style.

The method

Everything below is computed by the same solver the free tool runs, on its twenty starter foods at example prices (2,000 to 2,300 calories, 45 to 80 g of fat, at least 28 g of fibre, no food above four servings a day, half servings). The figures are a shape, not a quote: edit the prices to what you pay.

Choosing the vegan style drops 7 of the 20 foods (eggs, chicken thigh, whole milk, canned tuna, Greek yogurt, whey protein and cheddar) by name, leaving 13. The optimizer then finds the cheapest servings per day that still meet every bound.

What it costs

Protein minimumCheapest per dayPer week
80 g$1.79$12.56
100 g$1.93$13.51
120 g$2.18$15.26
130 g$2.38$16.66

The 100 g plan is lentils, rolled oats, peanut butter, rice, black beans and a little oil. Past that, more black beans join in and each extra 10 g costs more than the last. Above about 137 g a day this food list cannot meet the calorie cap at all (the tool also checks the half-serving rounding, so a real menu may stop slightly lower).

What the plan leaves out

It knows only calories, protein, carbs, fat, fibre, the optional sodium, calcium, iron and potassium bounds and the prices you typed. It does not know vitamin B12, which a vegan diet needs from fortified foods or a supplement, or amino-acid balance, allergies or taste. Ask a doctor or registered dietitian, not a solver, about those. It will not plan under 1,200 calories a day.

Questions

How much does a vegan high-protein diet cost per day?

On the 13 plant-based starter foods and example prices, the cheapest plan meeting 2,000 to 2,300 calories, 28 g of fibre and the fat bounds costs about $1.79 a day for 80 g of protein, $1.93 for 100 g and $2.18 for 120 g. Your prices will differ, so edit them.

Is vegan protein more expensive than a mixed diet?

Up to about 100 g a day, no: the cheapest mixed plan is also lentils, oats, rice and peanut butter, so the cost is the same $1.93. The gap shows above that, where a mixed plan can buy dense protein such as whey or chicken and a vegan plan has to keep adding beans and lentils.

Why does a vegan plan stop at about 137 g of protein?

Beans and lentils bring far more carbohydrate and calories per gram of protein than animal protein, so under a 2,300-calorie cap and four servings per food the plan runs out of room. Raising the calorie cap or the serving limit, or adding foods such as tofu or tempeh with their real prices, moves the ceiling.

how-to-eat-high-protein-on-a-budget.html.text:
← Cheapest meal plan optimizer

How to eat high-protein on a budget

"Cheap" and "high-protein" pull in different directions, and a grocery list built by instinct usually lands on the expensive side of both. The question is a puzzle with a known answer: the minimum-cost diet problem, one of the first linear programs ever solved. Give it foods, prices and targets, and it finds the cheapest combination that meets them.

Open the free cheapest meal plan optimizer

The method

1. Price one serving of each food. Use what you pay, and take calories, protein, carbs, fat and fibre from the label for that serving.

2. Set the targets. A calorie range, a protein minimum, fat bounds and a fibre minimum. A maximum number of servings per food keeps the plan eatable.

3. Solve. The optimizer picks servings that meet every bound at the lowest total price, then rounds to whole or half servings.

4. Read the price of each target. Re-solving with a higher protein minimum shows what each extra 10 g costs, which is usually the most useful number on the page.

A worked example

Twenty starter foods at example prices, 2,000 to 2,300 calories, at least 45 g and at most 80 g of fat, at least 28 g of fibre, no food above its serving cap, half servings. Only the protein minimum changes.

Protein minimumCheapest per dayPer week
100 g$1.93$13.51
140 g$2.74$19.21
180 g$4.38$30.66

The first 100 g come from dried lentils and beans, oats and peanut butter. Beyond that the calorie cap binds, so the plan has to buy protein in a denser form, whey, chicken or yogurt, and the price per extra gram rises. Run it on your own prices: the shape is the point, not these figures.

What the plan leaves out

It knows only calories, protein, carbs, fat and fibre and the prices you typed: not vitamins, minerals, allergies, taste, pack sizes or sales. The cheapest plan is often repetitive. It is not medical or dietary advice and will not plan under 1,200 calories a day.

Questions

How much does it cost to eat 100 g of protein a day?

On the starter foods and example prices, the cheapest plan that meets 2,000 to 2,300 calories, 100 g of protein, 28 g of fibre and the fat bounds costs about $1.93 a day, built from lentils, oats, peanut butter, rice and a little oil. Your prices will differ, so edit them.

Why does the cost jump as the protein target rises?

Cheap protein comes from dried beans and lentils, but they also bring a lot of carbohydrate and calories, so once the calorie cap binds the plan has to switch to denser protein such as whey, chicken or yogurt, which cost more per gram.

Can I add my own foods and prices?

Yes. Paste one line per food: name, price per serving, calories, protein, carbs, fat, fibre and an optional maximum servings per day. Take the nutrition from the label for the serving you are pricing.

CHEAPEST MEAL PLAN OPTIMIZER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

What is the cheapest way to hit your protein and calories?

List the foods you can buy with a price and nutrition per serving, set your targets, and a linear-programming solver finds the lowest-cost servings per day that meet them. It also tells you what each extra target costs, so you can see where the money goes.

The starter list uses approximate generic nutrition and example prices: edit every price to what you pay. New to this? Read how to eat high-protein on a budget, with a worked example, a cheap vegan version, what a $2 to $5 daily budget buys, or what one more gram of protein costs.

1. Foods

Add common foods to the list

Tick foods and add them: approximate generic nutrition with example prices. Replace each price with what you pay.

2. Daily targets

Add your foods and targets, then click Find the cheapest plan.

Your food list, prices and targets are remembered on this device only (browser local storage), so you can update prices each week.

Cheapest plan

FoodServings / dayCost / day

Nutrition of the plan

NutrientPlanYour bounds

What each target costs

    Cost as the protein minimum rises

    Protein minimumCheapest cost / day

    What a budget buys

    The other way round: the most protein each daily budget can reach while calories, fat, fiber and your other bounds still hold (your protein minimum is set aside here).

    Budget / dayMost protein

    What variety costs

    The cheapest plan is often a few foods. This caps the share of the day's calories any one food may supply and shows the cost and the number of foods used, with your other bounds unchanged.

    Most calories from one foodCheapest cost / dayFoods used

    A different menu each day

    The cheapest plan repeats every day. This plans the week day by day, charging more for a food each time it has already appeared, so the staples rotate while every bound still holds. Costs are at your real prices.

    DayFoods (servings)Cost

    What protein costs, food by food

    Your listed price per 100 g of protein and per 1,000 calories, cheapest protein first, ignoring every other bound. The plan can use a dearer protein for the calories, fibre or minerals it brings, so compare with the plan above.

    FoodPer 100 g proteinPer 1,000 kcalIn plan

    Foods left out: what price would earn a place?

    The price per serving at which each food the plan skips would start to be used, with everything else unchanged. Watch for sales near these.

    FoodYour priceUsed belowDrop needed

    Foods in the plan: how far can the price rise?

    The price per serving above which each food in the plan would be dropped for something else, with everything else unchanged. A food far above today's price is safe to keep buying through a price rise; one close to it is the first to swap out.

    FoodYour priceKept up toRise allowed

    Foods in the plan: what does losing one cost?

    The cheapest plan with each food taken off the list, everything else unchanged. Use it when you are tired of a food or cannot get it: the extra is what the swap costs per day. "Not possible" means your targets cannot be met without it.

    FoodCheapest plan without itExtra per day

    Compare with what you eat now

    Type what you eat in a day, one food per line with its servings (for example Rice 3). Foods are matched to your list by name. It shows what that day costs, which of your bounds it misses, and how much the plan above saves. Nothing is uploaded.

    Shopping list for the week

    FoodServings / weekPacks to buyLeft overAt the till

    How it works

    Model: choose servings x for each food to minimise the sum of price times servings, subject to each nutrient total staying within your bounds and each food staying under its serving cap. That is a linear program, solved with a two-phase simplex that cannot cycle.

    Whole and half servings: a continuous answer can say 1.37 servings of oats, so when you pick a step the solver uses branch and bound to find the cheapest plan in that step, and shows how far it is from the continuous lower bound.

    What each target costs: it re-solves with one minimum raised (by 100 kcal, 10 g of protein, 10 g of carbs or fat, or 5 g of fibre) and reports the extra cost. The rule-of-thumb comparison keeps adding the food that closes the most of the remaining shortfall per dollar.

    Not modelled: vitamins and minerals, allergies, taste and variety beyond the serving caps, cooking time, waste, pack sizes and sales. The cheapest plan is often monotonous; lower the caps or drop foods to see what variety costs. Unverified against real shopping: checked against exhaustive search on 60 random small menus and by an independent verifier on every plan.

    Common questions

    How do I make the cheapest meal plan that still hits my protein and calories?

    List the foods you can buy with the price of one serving and the nutrition in that serving, set a calorie range, a protein minimum and any fat, carb or fibre bounds, and the optimizer finds the servings per day with the lowest cost that meets all of them. It solves a linear program, the classic minimum-cost diet problem, then rounds to whole or half servings with branch and bound.

    Are the prices and nutrition numbers real?

    The starter foods carry approximate generic nutrition and example prices only. Prices vary by store, region and week, so edit the price on every line to what you pay, and check the nutrition against the label of what you actually buy. The result is only as good as the numbers you put in.

    Why is the cheapest plan so repetitive?

    Because a cost minimiser has no taste. If lentils and oats are the cheapest way to get calories and protein, it will use a lot of them. Lower the maximum servings per food, delete foods you will not eat, or add foods you like, and rerun it to see what variety costs.

    What does 'extra cost per 10 g of protein' mean?

    It is how much more the cheapest plan costs per day if you raise the protein minimum by 10 g, holding everything else. A target that adds nothing is not binding on this menu.

    Why will it not build a plan under 1,200 calories?

    A very low intake needs a clinician or registered dietitian, not an optimizer. The tool refuses to plan below 1,200 calories a day, and it is not suitable for children, pregnancy, eating disorders, diabetes or other medical conditions.

    Is this nutrition or medical advice?

    No. It does arithmetic on the numbers you give it. It does not know your health, allergies or needs, and it is not a substitute for a doctor or registered dietitian.

    Is my food list uploaded or stored?

    It is never uploaded. Everything runs in your browser, nothing is sent to a server and there are no accounts. So your prices are still there next week, your food list and targets are remembered on this device only (browser local storage); click Forget saved data to remove them. To send your list to someone else, use Copy share link (it puts the list in the address, which only your browser sees) or download the plan as a CSV.

what-does-one-more-gram-of-protein-cost..text:
← Cheapest meal plan optimizer

What does one more gram of protein cost?

The cost of a protein target is not a straight line. The optimizer's "extra cost of each target" readout re-solves the plan with the minimum raised by a small step and reports the difference: the marginal price of protein at the point you are at. That number tells you whether a bigger target is nearly free or the expensive part of your budget.

Open the free cheapest meal plan optimizer

The method

Everything below is computed by the same solver the free tool runs, on its twenty starter foods at example prices (2,000 to 2,300 calories, 45 to 80 g of fat, at least 28 g of fibre, no food above four servings a day, half servings). The figures are a shape, not a quote: edit the prices to what you pay.

What 10 more grams cost, by starting point

Protein minimumCheapest dayExtra for +10 g
80 g$1.79$0.07
100 g$1.93$0.08
120 g$2.18$0.18
140 g$2.74$0.35
160 g$3.52$0.36
180 g$4.38$0.48

Raising a low target is nearly free because the cheapest foods already carry it. Past roughly 120 g the plan runs out of cheap protein inside the calorie cap and has to buy denser sources, so each extra 10 g costs several times as much. Doubling the target from 80 g to 160 g more than doubles the bill.

What the plan leaves out

It knows only the nutrients you give it and the prices you typed: not vitamins, allergies, taste, pack sizes or sales. The marginal figure is for one small step from a given target and shifts as the plan changes. It is not medical or dietary advice and will not plan under 1,200 calories a day.

Questions

How much does 10 more grams of protein cost per day?

It depends where you start. On the starter foods at example prices, raising the minimum by 10 g adds about 7 cents a day at 80 g, 18 cents at 120 g and 48 cents at 180 g. Edit the prices to yours.

Why does protein get more expensive the more you ask for?

The cheapest protein per gram (lentils, oats, peanut butter) is used first. Once the calorie cap is reached, the plan must swap in denser, dearer sources such as whey, chicken and yogurt, so each extra gram costs more than the one before.

What is a marginal cost in a meal plan?

The extra cost of tightening one bound by a small step while re-solving for the cheapest plan. It is not the price of any one food: it is the price of moving the whole plan.

what-protein-does-a-grocery-budget-buy.h.text:
← Cheapest meal plan optimizer

How much protein does a daily food budget buy?

Most diet tools ask what you want to eat and then tell you the bill. If your grocery money is the fixed number, the useful question is the other way round: given this much a day, what is the most protein I can get? The optimizer's "what a budget buys" table answers it.

Open the free cheapest meal plan optimizer

The method

Everything below is computed by the same solver the free tool runs, on its twenty starter foods at example prices (2,000 to 2,300 calories, 45 to 80 g of fat, at least 28 g of fibre, no food above four servings a day, half servings). The figures are a shape, not a quote: edit the prices to what you pay.

The solver maximises protein subject to the daily spend, with the other bounds held. Figures are the continuous optimum, before rounding to half servings, so treat them as a ceiling you can approach.

What a budget buys

Daily budgetMost protein
$2.00109.8 g
$3.00149.2 g
$4.00175.4 g
$5.00196.2 g

The first dollars buy lentils, oats and peanut butter, the cheapest protein per cent. Later dollars go on denser sources such as whey, chicken and yogurt, which cost more per gram but fit inside the calorie cap. The same table for a vegan food list stalls near 137 g (see the vegan plan): more money cannot help once there is no room left.

What the plan leaves out

It knows only the nutrients you give it and the prices you typed: not vitamins, allergies, taste, pack sizes or sales. The cheapest or highest-protein plan is often repetitive; the tool can also cap the share of calories from one food. It is not medical or dietary advice and will not plan under 1,200 calories a day.

Questions

How much protein can I get for $2 a day?

On the starter foods and example prices, a $2 daily budget reaches about 110 g of protein inside 2,000 to 2,300 calories, the fat bounds and 28 g of fibre. That is the continuous optimum before rounding to half servings, so a real menu lands a little lower. Edit the prices to yours.

Does doubling the budget double the protein?

No. On these foods $2 reaches about 110 g, $3 about 149 g, $4 about 175 g and $5 about 196 g. Each extra dollar buys less protein than the one before, because the cheap protein is used first and the calorie cap forces a switch to denser, dearer sources.

Why does the budget view differ from the cost view?

They are the same model asked in opposite directions. The cost view fixes a protein target and finds the cheapest plan; the budget view fixes the spend and finds the most protein. The budget view is the one to use when your grocery money is the fixed number.
